newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-WEIS USES PERFECT TIMING TO WIN AT LAST.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-WEIS USES PERFECT TIMING TO WIN AT LAST.

text.p: German Heinz Weis seized with perfect timing on Sunday his last chance to win a major title by taking the hammer gold at the world championships.
The 34-year-old veteran had to wait until his final attempt to seize the lead.
"Those were my last world championships," he said afterwards. "I simply had to win."

Weis was second to Ukraine's Andrei Skvaruk when he threw the hammer for the last time, yelling as he released the implement. It landed at 81.78 metres, giving him the victory he had been chasing for so long.
"I nearly lost my voice but it was worth it," he said.

Skvaruk had been seemingly out of medal contention when he moved in front with his sixth and final throw of 81.46 metres, which eventually earned him silver. Russian Vasiliy Sidorenko took bronze with 80.76 metres.
"To win, you have to be the best when it matters most," said Sidorenko. "Today (Sunday), it was on the final try."
There was disappointment for Olympic champion Balazs Kiss of Hungary, who had to settle for fourth place with 79.96 metres.

Weis had warmed up for Athens with a remarkable 83.04 metres at the German championships in Frankfurt last June. Not only did he better his personal record but it was also the eighth best throw in the history of the sport and the best since 1992.

"Since Frankfurt, I knew I could win," said Weis, whose chances received a boost when Uzbek Andrey Abduvaliyev, the winner of the last two world championships, ended eighth in his qualifying group and failed to make it to the final.
Weis, who won the World Cup in 1989, has consistently been among the best throwers but his best result so far in world championships was a third place in 1991 in Tokyo.
He thought about giving up when his trainer and close friend Rudi Hars died last year but eventually decided to carry on with Bernhard Riedle, who taught him a new approach to competition.
"He learned me how to take high risks and still retain a perfect throw, which was the key to my victory," Weis said on Sunday.
The final started in low-key fashion with modest performances but the standard increased gradually to produce an exciting finale.

"This was the most interesting competition of my career," said Skvaruk after claiming an unexpected second place. "The start of the final showed how nervous we were and how many of us were capable of getting a medal."
Weis stayed in the stadium for nearly half an hour after his triumph, chatting and signing autographs.
"For 20 years, I've made sacrifices and invested everything I had hoping this moment would come," he said. "I had to wait a long time but I don't care. Now it's here."
